artifact.recommendation: Adopt continuous transaction-log backups at intervals of 15 minutes or less, weekly full database backups, and lifecycle tiering. Keep recent weekly fulls and logs in warm storage for operational recovery; retain the recovery chain needed for each month-end in cold storage for 12 months; and run automated integrity checks plus quarterly timed restore drills.
reasoning: This is the only option that directly satisfies the 15-minute database RPO: daily full backups alone cannot, while uniform 30-day retention violates the 12-month month-end requirement.
Weekly fulls substantially reduce the largest cost component: daily full database backups currently account for 72% of backup storage cost.

A weekly cycle consumes roughly 1 full-backup equivalent plus 0.42 equivalents of logs, versus 7 daily-full equivalents, before accounting for retained month-end chains. This indicates ample potential to exceed the required 35% total cost reduction.
The demonstrated weekly-full-plus-logs restore time of 76 minutes leaves 44 minutes of margin against the two-hour RTO, including the cold tier's maximum stated 20-minute retrieval delay.
Compliance requires recoverability of month-end records for 12 months, not retention of every daily full image, so month-end recovery points can be preserved without the current policy's redundancy.
Customer documents already have independent versioning and lifecycle tiering, making database backup redesign the dominant remaining cost lever.
considerations: Set log shipping or upload frequency below 15 minutes—such as every 5 minutes—to leave monitoring and ingestion margin around the RPO.
Define immutable month-end recovery sets that include a usable full backup and every required log segment; retaining isolated logs or snapshots may not provide recoverability.
Keep enough recent backups in warm storage to handle common incidents without cold retrieval, while placing older month-end recovery sets in cold storage.
Test both warm-tier and cold-tier restores, validate backup integrity automatically, and alert on missing log segments.
Confirm whether the two-hour RTO begins at incident declaration and includes cold retrieval, decryption, provisioning, replay, validation, and application reconnection.
Apply the proposed policy to the database; preserve the independently managed document-object lifecycle unless a separate review identifies deficiencies.
assumptions: Continuous logs can be captured and durably stored no less frequently than every 15 minutes.
The 76-minute drill is representative of current production data volume and includes log replay, or sufficient scaling margin can be demonstrated.
Cold-tier retrieval delay is additive to the measured restore duration, yielding approximately 96 minutes in the stated worst case.
Compliance permits reconstructing month-end state from a full backup and logs rather than requiring a standalone month-end full image.
No legal hold, contractual term, or regional rule requires daily database recovery points for the full year.
risks: A missing or corrupt log segment can break point-in-time recovery and invalidate later month-end recovery points.
Restore duration may increase as database size and log volume grow, eroding the current RTO margin.
Cold-tier retrieval delays may exceed the stated maximum operationally or involve request fees that weaken projected savings.
The 35% savings target is not proven until current inventory, retained recovery-chain sizes, tier minimum durations, retrieval charges, and replication overhead are modeled.
Deleting legacy daily fulls before replacement month-end recovery sets are validated could create a compliance gap.
Backup credentials or repositories without immutability and access separation remain vulnerable to ransomware or operator error.
evidence_needed: A 12-month cost model comparing the current policy with weekly fulls, continuous logs, required month-end chains, replicas, cold-tier minimum-duration charges, and expected retrieval fees.
An inventory of backup sizes, compression and deduplication ratios, daily change rate, database growth forecast, and existing log-backup costs.
A timed end-to-end restore from cold storage at production scale, including provisioning, retrieval, decryption, log replay, validation, and application availability.
Written compliance confirmation defining month-end recoverability, acceptable reconstruction methods, retention clock, immutability, and deletion requirements.
Monitoring evidence showing sustained log-backup intervals within the RPO and successful automated recovery-chain validation.
A documented transition plan that preserves all required historical month-end recovery points while redundant daily fulls expire safely.

citations.claim: Daily full database backups account for 72% of current backup storage cost.
Point-in-time recovery logs consume about 6% of one daily full backup per day.
Compliance requires 12 months of month-end recoverability but does not require daily full images.
A weekly-full-plus-logs restore completed in 76 minutes.
Cold storage is 68% cheaper per GB and can add up to 20 minutes of retrieval delay.
Document objects already use independent versioning and lifecycle tiering, leaving database backups as the main cost lever.
The required database objectives are RPO no greater than 15 minutes, RTO no greater than two hours, and at least 35% monthly backup-storage savings.

artifact.recommendation: Use continuous database log backups at intervals of 15 minutes or less, weekly full backups, cold-tiering for older backups, and mandatory restore testing. Retain sufficient logs for point-in-time recovery, preserve month-end recoverability for 12 months, and keep document-object lifecycle policies unchanged.
reasoning: This is the only option that directly supports the database RPO of at most 15 minutes while substantially reducing dependence on daily full backups.
Weekly fulls replace most daily fulls, which currently account for 72 percent of backup storage cost; cold-tiering older recovery sets adds further savings.

The demonstrated 76-minute restore time leaves 44 minutes of RTO headroom. Even the cold tier's maximum 20-minute retrieval delay would produce an indicative 96-minute recovery, within the two-hour objective.
Compliance requires 12-month recoverability of month-end records, not 12 months of daily full images, so the policy can reduce backup frequency without reducing required compliance coverage.

A 30-day blanket retention policy would violate the stated 12-month month-end recoverability requirement, while negotiating storage pricing alone does not reliably establish the required 35 percent savings.
considerations: Define explicit retention periods for weekly fulls, transaction logs, and month-end recovery sets so every retained month-end can actually be restored.
Schedule frequent automated restore validation plus quarterly timed drills covering both hot and cold-tier recovery paths.
Ensure log backups are copied off-system and monitored for gaps; continuous logs are only useful when the recovery chain remains intact.
Model storage, retrieval, API-operation, and restore-egress charges before final rollout.
Use immutable or isolated backup copies and documented encryption/key-recovery controls.
assumptions: The 76-minute drill is representative of production data volume and includes database validation.
Cold-tier retrieval delay is additive to the measured restore duration, yielding an indicative worst case of 96 minutes.
Weekly fulls and their required logs can preserve each mandated month-end recovery point for 12 months.
The database cost reduction from eliminating most daily fulls, combined with tiering, is sufficient to reduce total monthly backup storage cost by at least 35 percent.
Customer-uploaded documents remain protected by their existing independent versioning and lifecycle policy.
risks: A broken or missing log segment could prevent point-in-time recovery or make a retained month-end unrecoverable.
Data growth, bandwidth contention, decryption, or cold-tier variability could push restore time beyond two hours.
Over-aggressive log expiration could leave full backups present but unusable for required recovery points.
Cold-tier retrieval and transaction charges could reduce realized savings.
The evidence does not provide a complete cost model or specify whether the prior drill included cold retrieval and end-to-end application validation.
evidence_needed: A 12-month cost projection comparing the current policy with weekly fulls, retained logs, month-end recovery sets, and hot/cold-tier charges.
A precise retention map proving that every required month-end recovery point remains recoverable for 12 months.
An end-to-end restore drill from cold storage at projected production scale, including integrity and application-level validation.
Monitoring evidence showing log-backup frequency remains at or below 15 minutes and that chain gaps trigger alerts.
Written confirmation that the proposed month-end recovery representation satisfies compliance requirements.

Point-in-time recovery logs consume about 6 percent of one daily full backup per day.

strengths: Selects the option best aligned with the 15-minute RPO, two-hour RTO, and 12-month month-end recoverability requirement.
Correctly identifies daily full backups as the principal cost-reduction lever and preserves the independently managed document lifecycle.
Recognizes that full backups and transaction logs must form complete, validated recovery chains.
Explicitly calls for integrity monitoring, gap alerts, immutable or isolated copies, and timed warm- and cold-tier restore drills.
Clearly distinguishes promising cost-reduction potential from the need for a complete cost model before claiming compliance with the 35% target.
Identifies transition risk and the need to preserve historical month-end recovery points while legacy backups expire.
weaknesses: The precise retention schedule is not defined: warm retention, weekly-full retention, log expiration, month-end chain composition, and cold-tier duration remain unspecified.
The RTO comparison treats the 20-minute cold retrieval delay as simply additive to the 76-minute drill without evidence that all other drill conditions match the proposed architecture.
The recommendation does not define whether month-end recovery sets will use dedicated monthly fulls, selected weekly fulls plus bounded logs, or another reconstruction method.
Operational recovery testing frequency is described inconsistently as automated validation plus quarterly drills without specifying what is restored automatically or how success is measured.
unsupported: The claim that the proposed design has ample potential to exceed 35% total monthly storage-cost savings is directionally plausible but not demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

The indicative 96-minute cold-tier recovery assumes retrieval is the only additional latency and that retrieval, provisioning, replay, validation, and application reconnection do not overlap or introduce further delays.
The assertion that this is the only option directly satisfying the RPO assumes the listed daily-full option excludes transaction-log backups; the option wording does not explicitly state that.

The reports imply that existing document protection should remain unchanged, but the evidence establishes only independent versioning and tiering, not that its recovery objectives or controls are adequate.
missing: A quantified steady-state cost model including backup sizes, compression, deduplication, replication, growth, cold-tier minimum-duration charges, retrieval fees, and retained month-end chains.
An explicit retention matrix for every backup artifact and storage tier, including deletion dependencies.
Evidence that the 76-minute drill included production-scale provisioning, decryption, full log replay, integrity validation, and application availability.
A demonstrated worst-case RPO calculation covering transaction commit, log rotation, upload, durable replication, monitoring detection, and retry time.
Written compliance confirmation covering reconstruction from logs, retention-clock semantics, legal holds, immutability, regional requirements, and deletion rules.
A transition and rollback procedure with acceptance gates before legacy daily full backups are removed.
Capacity projections showing that database and log growth will not erode the RTO during the policy horizon.
incorrect_assumptions: Treating a backup interval of exactly 15 minutes as sufficient may be incorrect because capture, transfer, and durable-storage latency can make actual data loss exceed 15 minutes.
Assuming the 76-minute restore remains representative as data size and log volume grow is not established.
Assuming cold-tier retrieval always adds no more than 20 minutes operationally may overlook queueing, object hydration, request batching, and provider exceptions.
Assuming reconstructed month-end state satisfies compliance is unverified.
Assuming elimination of most daily fulls plus tiering necessarily achieves at least 35% total monthly backup-storage savings is premature.
critical_risks: A single missing, corrupt, or cryptographically inaccessible log segment can invalidate point-in-time recovery and one or more retained month-end recovery points.
Deleting legacy backups before replacement chains pass end-to-end validation could create an irreversible compliance and recovery gap.
Actual end-to-end cold restore time could exceed two hours despite the simple 96-minute estimate.
Realized savings could miss the mandatory 35% threshold after accounting for long-lived logs, replicas, minimum storage periods, retrieval, and operation charges.
Compromised backup credentials, encryption keys, or non-immutable repositories could make the entire policy ineffective during ransomware or operator-error incidents.
recommended_changes: Replace the qualitative savings claim with a 12-month monthly cost table and require modeled savings comfortably above 35% before migration.
Specify a concrete retention matrix for warm weekly fulls, operational logs, immutable month-end recovery sets, cold storage, and deletion dependencies.
Use a log-backup cadence below 15 minutes and define RPO measurement from the latest committed transaction to durable recoverability, including retries and alerting.
Run a production-scale cold-tier restore before approval and measure the complete incident-to-application-available timeline.
Obtain written compliance approval for the exact month-end reconstruction method and legal-hold behavior.
Adopt a staged migration in which legacy daily fulls expire only after every required historical and new month-end point has a validated replacement recovery chain.
Define automated chain-validation frequency, quarterly drill scenarios, success thresholds, ownership, escalation, and remediation deadlines.

strengths: Both reports select the option best aligned with the stated RPO, RTO, compliance, and cost objectives.
The recommendations correctly preserve 12 months of month-end recoverability rather than unnecessary daily full images.
They appropriately emphasize complete recovery chains, monitoring for missing logs, restore testing, immutability, and a safe transition.
Claims are generally traceable to the supplied evidence, and both reports explicitly identify the missing cost model and cold-tier restore test.
They correctly leave the independently managed document-object lifecycle policy outside the database redesign.
weaknesses: The reports recommend adoption before proving the mandatory 35 percent total monthly storage-cost reduction; the evidence supports potential savings, not compliance with the cost constraint.

The 96-minute cold-recovery estimate treats the 20-minute retrieval delay as simply additive to the 76-minute drill without establishing that the drill and cold restore otherwise have equivalent scope, throughput, and data volume.
The retention design remains conceptual: neither report specifies which full backup anchors each month-end, exactly which logs are retained, or when each component expires.
Research-1's weekly-cycle calculation is useful but compares one week's newly generated backup volume, not steady-state retained storage cost across the required 12 months.
The stated confidence values are high relative to unresolved mandatory cost and end-to-end RTO evidence.
unsupported: That weekly fulls, logs, and tiering will achieve at least 35 percent reduction in total monthly backup storage cost.
That the last restore drill remains representative of current and projected production scale.
That cold-tier recovery takes approximately 96 minutes in the worst case.
That the 76-minute drill included all RTO stages, such as provisioning, decryption, validation, and application reconnection.
That reconstructing month-end state from a full backup and logs is acceptable to compliance.
That the cold tier's stated retrieval delay is a guaranteed maximum under operational conditions.
missing: A quantified steady-state cost comparison covering database fulls, logs, month-end chains, replicas, compression, deduplication, minimum storage periods, retrieval fees, and growth.
Explicit warm-storage retention periods and a precise month-end recovery-chain expiration schedule.
Clarification of whether logs are incremental from the latest full, how log-chain continuity crosses weekly fulls, and whether independent month-end recovery sets are required.
An end-to-end production-scale cold restore measurement against the formal start and end points of the two-hour RTO.
Defined backup-log frequency and alert thresholds that account for scheduling, upload, and durability latency—not merely a nominal 15-minute interval.
Recovery objectives and compliance validation for customer-uploaded documents, even if their existing lifecycle policy remains unchanged.
Transition acceptance criteria and rollback steps before legacy daily full backups are allowed to expire.
incorrect_assumptions: A nominal log-backup interval of exactly 15 minutes necessarily guarantees an RPO of at most 15 minutes; execution and durability delays can exceed the objective.
Cold retrieval delay can be added directly to the prior drill time without other cold-path effects.
Eliminating most daily fulls necessarily produces the required total cost reduction despite logs, retained month-end chains, replication, and storage-tier charges.
The phrase 'continuous log backup' is compatible with periodic uploads without defining when a log is considered durably recoverable.
critical_risks: A single missing, corrupt, or expired log segment can invalidate point-in-time recovery and multiple retained month-end recovery points.
Rolling out before validating the cost model could fail a hard decision constraint despite materially reducing raw storage volume.
Cold-tier restores may exceed the RTO because the prior 76-minute drill does not establish full cold-path, application-ready recovery time.
Premature expiration of legacy backups could create an irreversible 12-month compliance gap.
Ransomware, credential compromise, or key loss could render backups unusable unless immutability, isolation, and independent key recovery are implemented and tested.
recommended_changes: Make adoption conditional on a cost model demonstrating at least 35 percent monthly savings with conservative growth and fee assumptions.
Replace the 96-minute assertion with a provisional estimate and require a measured cold-tier, application-ready restore before final approval.
Specify a concrete retention matrix for weekly fulls, logs, warm copies, cold month-end sets, expiration dates, and chain dependencies.
Set the operational log-backup target below 15 minutes and define monitoring against durable completion time.
State formal RTO boundaries and test every included stage at projected production scale.
Obtain written compliance approval for reconstructed month-end recovery points and document immutability, legal-hold, and deletion requirements.
Lower confidence until the mandatory cost threshold and end-to-end cold restore are demonstrated.

attacks: The recommendation is premature because it has not demonstrated the mandatory 35% reduction in total monthly backup-storage cost; lower raw backup volume is not equivalent to lower billed cost.
The weekly calculation compares backup generation over one week, not 12-month steady-state retention including month-end chains, replication, compression, tier minimums, operations, and growth.

The claimed 96-minute cold restore is an unjustified arithmetic sum. The 76-minute drill may exclude retrieval, provisioning, decryption, replay at projected scale, validation, and application reconnection.
A nominal 15-minute log interval does not guarantee a 15-minute RPO because scheduling, log closure, transfer, replication, retries, and durability confirmation add latency.
The month-end retention design is not implementable as stated: it does not identify each anchor full, required log range, cross-full chain behavior, expiration dependencies, or legal-hold treatment.
Long-lived log chains create correlated failure: one missing, corrupt, expired, or undecryptable segment can invalidate multiple month-end recovery points.

Compliance acceptance of reconstructed month-end state is assumed rather than established; recoverability may require dedicated images, immutability, specific retention-clock semantics, or regional controls.
The evidence does not establish that cold retrieval delay is a guaranteed maximum or that hydration throughput and request batching are covered.
The recommendation to leave document protection unchanged overreaches evidence showing only versioning and tiering, not adequate recovery objectives, immutability, or tested restoration.
Confidence above 0.9 is inconsistent with unresolved proof for two hard constraints: cost savings and end-to-end cold-path RTO.
falsifiers: A conservative 12-month billed-cost model shows savings below 35% in any expected growth scenario after replicas, retained logs, month-end chains, minimum-duration charges, API fees, and retrieval costs.
A production-scale cold-tier drill exceeds two hours from incident declaration to validated application availability.
Observed age of the newest durably recoverable transaction exceeds 15 minutes during ordinary delay, retry, failover, or backlog conditions.
Written compliance guidance rejects reconstruction from a weekly full plus logs or requires daily recovery points, dedicated month-end images, or controls absent from the design.
Recovery-chain validation finds that any retained month-end cannot be restored independently because of an expired, missing, corrupt, or inaccessible log or key.
Projected database or log growth pushes replay and validation time beyond the available RTO margin during the policy horizon.
Provider terms or operational measurements show cold retrieval can exceed 20 minutes or requires materially higher charges than modeled.
Document restore testing shows the existing object lifecycle cannot satisfy applicable recovery or compliance requirements.
evidence_gaps: A monthly, steady-state cost baseline and 12-month forecast for both current and proposed policies, using actual compression, deduplication, replication, growth, minimum-duration, operation, retrieval, and egress charges.
A precise retention matrix identifying full-backup anchors, log ranges, warm and cold copies, month-end sets, expiration dates, deletion dependencies, immutability, and legal-hold behavior.
A measured production-scale cold restore covering formal RTO start and end points, provisioning, retrieval, decryption, complete replay, integrity checks, application reconnection, and validation.
Telemetry proving the worst-case commit-to-durable-recoverability interval remains at most 15 minutes, including retries, replication, detection, alerting, and failover.
Written compliance approval for the exact month-end reconstruction method, retention-clock semantics, regional requirements, immutability, deletion, and key retention.
Evidence that the 76-minute drill used representative current and projected data volumes and included all stages counted by the RTO.
Provider evidence or measurements supporting the 20-minute cold retrieval bound under realistic object counts, concurrency, queueing, and incident conditions.
A staged migration and rollback plan with validated replacement chains before any legacy daily full expires.
Defined automated validation scope, drill frequency, success thresholds, ownership, escalation, and remediation deadlines.
Recovery-objective and restore-test evidence for customer-uploaded documents before declaring their existing policy out of scope.

accepted_criticisms: The original recommendation was premature because the mandatory 35% reduction in total monthly backup-storage cost was not demonstrated.
The weekly backup-volume calculation does not establish 12-month steady-state billed cost after month-end retention, replication, compression, tier rules, fees, and growth.
The approximately 96-minute cold-restore estimate is provisional because the evidence does not show that the 76-minute drill covered all end-to-end RTO stages or projected scale.
A nominal 15-minute log-backup interval does not by itself guarantee a 15-minute RPO after transfer, retry, replication, and durability latency.
The proposed month-end retention design lacks a concrete matrix of full anchors, required log segments, expiration dependencies, immutability, key retention, and legal-hold treatment.
Long-lived log-chain dependencies create correlated recoverability risk from missing, corrupt, expired, or inaccessible segments or keys.
Compliance acceptance of reconstructing month-end state from a weekly full and logs is not established.
Leaving document protection unchanged should be conditional on a separate confirmation of its recovery and compliance requirements.
Confidence above 0.9 was unjustified while the mandatory cost threshold and end-to-end cold-path RTO remained unproven.
rejected_criticisms: The evidence fails to establish any 20-minute upper bound for cold retrieval. Evidence e5 expressly states a retrieval delay of up to 20 minutes; what remains unproven is whether that bound applies under the proposed production architecture and complete RTO measurement.

The weekly-full-and-log option should be rejected outright. The visible evidence still makes it the strongest candidate: it addresses point-in-time recovery, removes most daily fulls from the dominant cost component, supports month-end retention, and has a successful 76-minute restore precedent. The evidence supports conditional validation, not rejection.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select weekly full database backups, sub-15-minute transaction-log backup targets, lifecycle tiering, and tested month-end recovery chains as the preferred design, but do not approve migration or expire legacy daily fulls yet. Final adoption must be gated on a conservative 12-month billed-cost model demonstrating at least 35% monthly savings, a production-scale cold-tier restore completing within two hours from incident declaration to validated application availability, telemetry proving commit-to-durable-recoverability stays within 15 minutes, a precise retention and dependency matrix, and written compliance approval of the reconstruction, immutability, legal-hold, regional, deletion, and key-retention controls. Review document recovery requirements separately before affirming that its existing lifecycle is adequate.
reasons: The candidate architecture is directionally superior to daily fulls or blanket 30-day retention, but two mandatory constraints—cost reduction and complete cold-path RTO—are not yet proven.

Daily fulls represent 72% of current backup-storage cost and cold storage is materially cheaper, so achieving the savings target is plausible, but raw-volume reductions cannot substitute for billed-cost modeling.
The 76-minute drill is useful evidence of feasibility, but adding 20 minutes arithmetically does not establish complete incident-to-application recovery at projected scale.
A cadence below 15 minutes plus durability-based monitoring is necessary to preserve margin for operational latency.
Validated, immutable recovery sets and staged migration are necessary because dependent log chains can fail across multiple retained month-end points.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation was premature because the evidence shows savings potential but does not demonstrate the mandatory 35% reduction in total monthly backup-storage cost.

The weekly generation calculation is not a substitute for a 12-month steady-state billed-cost model covering retained month-end chains, replication, compression, growth, tier minimums, operations, retrieval, and egress.

The approximately 96-minute cold restore is only a provisional estimate; the evidence does not establish that the 76-minute drill included all RTO stages or that cold retrieval is the only added latency.
A nominal 15-minute log-backup interval does not guarantee a 15-minute RPO once closure, transfer, retries, replication, and durable confirmation are included.
The month-end retention design is not sufficiently specified to prove recoverability, expiration safety, legal-hold handling, or compliance acceptance.
Long log-chain dependencies create correlated recovery risk from missing, corrupt, expired, inaccessible, or undecryptable segments.
Compliance acceptance of reconstructed month-end states, including immutability, retention-clock, regional, deletion, and key-retention requirements, remains unverified.
The evidence does not establish that the stated cold retrieval delay is an operationally guaranteed maximum under representative scale, object count, batching, and incident conditions.
Leaving document protection unchanged is not fully supported merely by evidence of versioning and lifecycle tiering; its recovery and compliance adequacy still requires separate validation.
Confidence above 0.9 was too high while the mandatory cost threshold and end-to-end cold-path RTO remained unproven.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select weekly full database backups, sub-15-minute transaction-log targets, lifecycle tiering, and tested month-end recovery chains as the preferred design, but approve migration only conditionally. Before legacy daily fulls expire, require a conservative 12-month cost model demonstrating at least 35% monthly savings, a production-scale cold restore completing within two hours from incident declaration to validated application availability, telemetry proving commit-to-durable-recoverability stays within 15 minutes, a precise retention and dependency matrix, and written compliance approval. Preserve the document lifecycle temporarily, subject to a separate recovery and compliance validation.
reasons: The supplied evidence strongly favors the weekly-full-plus-logs architecture over daily fulls or blanket 30-day retention, but architectural preference is not proof that every hard constraint is met.

Daily fulls account for 72% of current storage cost and cold storage is materially cheaper, so achieving the savings target is plausible, but retained logs and month-end chains prevent deriving billed savings from the weekly generation ratio alone.
The 76-minute drill supports feasibility of the RTO, but its scope and representativeness are unspecified; adding 20 minutes does not establish a worst-case end-to-end result.
A cadence below 15 minutes provides operating margin, but only observed durable recoverability latency can establish compliance with the RPO.
The design can satisfy month-end retention only if every anchor, required log, encryption key, expiration dependency, and legal-hold rule is explicitly preserved and validated.
A staged, gated migration retains the likely benefits of the preferred option without asserting that unresolved mandatory constraints have already been satisfied.

artifact.decision: Choose the weekly-full-plus-continuous-log architecture as the preferred option, but do not grant final production approval or expire legacy daily fulls until all mandatory gates are proven.
artifact.action: Proceed with a staged validation and migration design using sub-15-minute log capture targets, weekly fulls, lifecycle tiering, and complete 12-month month-end recovery chains. Require a conservative billed-cost model, production-scale cold restore, durable-recoverability telemetry, explicit retention matrix, and written compliance approval before cutover or legacy-backup expiration.
reasons: This option best addresses the 15-minute RPO while reducing reliance on daily full backups, which constitute 72% of current backup-storage cost.
The supplied evidence makes a 35% cost reduction plausible but does not prove it in steady-state billed-cost terms; therefore unconditional adoption would violate a hard decision constraint.
The 76-minute weekly-full-plus-logs drill supports RTO feasibility, but its scope, scale, and relationship to cold retrieval are insufficient to prove an end-to-end two-hour RTO.

Twelve-month month-end recoverability can potentially be maintained without daily full images, but the required full anchors, logs, keys, expiration dependencies, and compliance controls remain unspecified.

A 30-day retention policy conflicts directly with the stated 12-month month-end requirement, while retaining daily fulls and negotiating price neither addresses the RPO on its face nor demonstrates the required savings.
Sub-15-minute scheduling is necessary because an exact 15-minute interval leaves no margin for closure, transfer, retries, replication, and durable confirmation.
evidence: Problem e1 states that daily full database backups account for 72% of current backup-storage cost.
Problem e2 states that point-in-time recovery logs average 6% of a daily full backup's storage per day.
Problem e3 states that compliance requires 12 months of month-end recoverability, not daily full images.
Problem e4 reports a 76-minute restore of a weekly full plus logs.
Problem e5 states that cold-tier storage costs 68% less per GB and has retrieval delay of up to 20 minutes.
Problem e6 states that documents are independently versioned and already lifecycle-tiered, making the database the dominant remaining cost lever.
Both rebuttals appropriately revise the recommendation from immediate adoption to gated, staged adoption and lower confidence because cost and complete cold-path RTO remain unproven.
Both reviews independently identify the missing steady-state cost model, end-to-end cold restore, exact retention matrix, durable RPO measurement, compliance approval, and safe transition plan.
rejected_alternatives: Keep daily full backups for one year and negotiate pricing: no evidence demonstrates at least 35% savings, and the option does not itself establish a 15-minute RPO.
Reduce all retention to 30 days: this contradicts the explicit requirement for 12 months of month-end recoverability.
Approve the weekly-full-plus-logs design immediately: the mandatory cost reduction and complete cold-path RTO have not been demonstrated.

Reject weekly fulls plus logs outright: the available evidence makes this the strongest candidate and includes a successful 76-minute restore precedent; the deficiencies justify validation gates, not abandonment.
Treat 76 plus 20 minutes as a proven 96-minute worst-case RTO: the artifacts do not establish equivalent scope, representative scale, or inclusion of every incident-to-application-ready stage.
minority: Research-1 and research-2 initially recommend adoption with confidence above 0.9, but their own assumptions and evidence-needed sections acknowledge that cost compliance, cold-path RTO, reconstruction compliance, and chain integrity are unresolved.

Review-1 questions whether the weekly-full option is uniquely capable of satisfying RPO because the daily-full option does not explicitly prohibit logs; this ambiguity does not make the daily-full option preferable because its savings remain unproven.
Rebuttal-1 distinguishes the stated 20-minute bound from whether that bound applies operationally to the proposed architecture; this is more precise than treating e5 as providing no bound at all.
unresolved: Whether the proposed policy reduces total monthly backup-storage cost by at least 35% under 12-month steady-state retention and expected growth.
Whether a production-scale cold restore completes within two hours from incident declaration through validated application availability.
Whether commit-to-durable-recoverability remains within 15 minutes during ordinary delay, retry, backlog, and failover conditions.
The exact full anchors, log ranges, cross-full dependencies, storage tiers, expiration dates, encryption-key retention, immutability, and legal-hold behavior for each month-end recovery point.
Whether compliance accepts reconstruction from a full plus logs and approves the proposed retention-clock, regional, deletion, and control semantics.
Whether the existing document lifecycle satisfies its own recovery and compliance requirements.
Whether the 76-minute drill represented current and projected production scale and included provisioning, decryption, complete replay, integrity validation, and application reconnection.
assumptions: The three listed options are candidates rather than authorization to waive any mandatory constraint.
Legacy daily fulls can remain temporarily while the preferred architecture is validated.
A log-backup target below 15 minutes is operationally possible, although this must be demonstrated.
The phrase 'up to 20 minutes' in e5 is a stated bound in the supplied evidence, not proof of an enforceable production guarantee under every incident condition.
Documents may remain temporarily under their existing lifecycle while their recovery and compliance adequacy is separately reviewed.
change_conditions: Grant final approval if conservative steady-state modeling demonstrates at least 35% monthly savings and measured production-scale tests prove both RPO and RTO under formal boundary definitions.
Reject or redesign the preferred option if modeled savings fall below 35% in expected growth scenarios.
Reject or redesign cold tiering if an end-to-end application-ready restore exceeds two hours.

Use dedicated month-end images or another approved structure if compliance rejects reconstruction from weekly fulls and logs.
Retain legacy daily fulls longer if replacement month-end chains cannot be independently validated before expiration.
Revise the document policy if separate testing shows its existing versioning and tiering do not satisfy applicable objectives.

Run a production-scale cold restore measuring incident declaration through provisioning, retrieval, decryption, replay, integrity checks, application reconnection, and validated availability.
Measure worst-case commit-to-durable-recoverability latency under retries, replication delays, backlog, and failover.

reasons: The weekly-full-plus-logs option is the strongest candidate because it supports point-in-time recovery, targets the dominant database cost lever, and can preserve 12 months of month-end recoverability.
